newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan recovery seen unaffected by Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan recovery seen unaffected by Deng's death.

text.p: Taiwan's economy should maintain its gradual recovery despite the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, although investment in the mainland may slow, officials and economists said on Thursday.
"We do not expect (Deng's death) to have too strong an impact on our economy," the economics ministry said in a statement.
"But the future changes of communist China's power structure and its policy change toward us may influence the development of cross-strait economic and trade relations," it said.
Trade with China has been a key engine in the island's recent economic growth, officials said.
Some 30,000 Taiwan-funded businesses have invested an estimated US$20 billion in China since Taipei began allowing indirect contact with the mainland in the mid 1980s.
Officials said Deng's death had long been expected and should not cause chaos on the mainland since Deng had retreated from China's power centre for years.
Taiwan and China have been diplomatic rivals since a Chinese civil war split them in 1949.
"Our expected gradual economic recovery should continue despite Deng's death," Chang Yao-tsung, the economics ministry's statistics director, told Reuters.
"No chaos is expected on the mainland, and communist China should continue to trade with us," said Chang.
A November government forecast said the island's gross domestic product in 1997 would grow 6.2 percent, up from an estimated 5.7 percent in 1996.

"The real impact (of Deng's death) won't be strong. Taiwan's economy should return to fundamentals, and is expected to recover this year," said Wu Hui-lin, senior economist at Chunghwa Institution for Economic Research.
Kao Ching-yuan, chief executive officer of Taiwan's top China investor, food giant President Enterprises, said: "Deng died, and the thing that everybody worried about has gone."
"It will have no impact on Taiwan's economy, whose performance this year should be better than last year," Kao told reporters.
However, the government called for caution in evaluating investment in China.

"Although the mainland economic opening policies will not go backward, the economics ministry urges Taiwan businessmen to take political risks into consideration when considering medium- to long-term investments," government spokesman Su Chi quoted economics minister Wang Chih-kang as saying.
Economist Wu said Taiwan businesses may become more cautious about investing in the mainland.
But Kao, who in August 1996 led a large Taiwan business delegation to Beijing and met with China's President Jiang Zemin, said most Taiwan investors had factored Deng's death into investment plans.
"Taiwan investments (in China) will not change," he said.
"Deng's death was something all businessmen were expecting, so there is no reason for them to be nervous," said Kao, who is also chairman of the Chinese National Federation of Industries.
Taiwan share prices shrugged off the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to close higher on Thursday, and analysts expected the market to seek fresh highs.
On Thursday the weighted index recovered from an early fall to close 21.19 points or 0.28 percent higher at 7,678.04.
